headline: LearnBoard: A UI that makes your AI remember you across sessions
summary: LearnBoard is a new UI that tackles the persistent problem of AI agents forgetting past interactions. It manages a structured LEARNING.md file, allowing AIs to retain context and preferences across sessions.
details: AI agents often forget context from previous sessions, forcing developers to repeatedly explain their stack, preferences, and past lessons. This constant re-explanation is a significant hidden cost in working with AI.

LearnBoard solves this by providing a management interface for a structured memory file called LEARNING.md. This file stores everything the AI learns about your workflow, patterns, and successful approaches.

The system operates as a Node.js server on port 4331, serving a web dashboard for your LEARNING.md file. It uses chokidar to watch the file and pushes real-time updates to the UI via Server-Sent Events.

Key features include a lessons table with confidence scores, category filters, and inline editing, a tools inventory bootstrapped from your environment, and a suggestions queue with a voting system for new ideas.

Designed to be read by AI, the structured Markdown format is unambiguous to language models. Confidence scores and session stats provide signals for the AI to weigh lessons, ensuring more informed decisions.

The AI can also write to the LEARNING.md file, enabling a continuous learning loop where lessons from successful sessions are stored and immediately reflected in the dashboard, improving future interactions.

LearnBoard operates fully locally with no cloud, sync, or account dependencies. The LEARNING.md file is plain text, easily readable, commit-able, and shareable, ensuring vendor independence and survivable architecture.

headline_marked: [[Debugging AI Coding Agents]] by inspecting prompts, tool calls, token usage, and cost
headline: Debugging AI Coding Agents by inspecting prompts, tool calls, token usage, and cost
summary: When AI coding agents fail, the visible error is rarely the whole story. Learn to inspect system prompts, tool calls, token usage, and costs to diagnose issues effectively.
details: When AI coding agents encounter errors, the visible problem often doesn't reveal the root cause. For agentic coding tools, simply guessing isn't enough; developers need to inspect the actual data an agent sends to the underlying model.

Key areas to inspect include the system prompt, which can override user instructions, and tool calling. Vaguely described tools, confusing parameter names, or schema issues can lead models to select incorrect tools or produce invalid arguments.

Tool call bugs can originate from the model, client, or provider adapter. For instance, a model might emit a tool call that the client renders as text, causing the agent to proceed as if the tool executed when it didn't.

A single file read, search result, or command output can add thousands of tokens to the next turn. If an agent suddenly becomes expensive or confused, checking the tool results fed back into the model is crucial.

Per-request token usage offers more insight than total session costs, differentiating between a generally expensive session and a specific tool result causing a spike. This granular view helps pinpoint inefficiencies.

Tools like ccglass act as a local proxy and dashboard, allowing developers to inspect the traffic of supported coding agents. It reveals exactly what agents send to the model, including prompts, tool schemas, and responses.

For generic OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic-compatible clients, a proxy-only mode can be used by pointing the client or IDE to a local base URL. This enables inspection of the exact request flow and turn-to-turn diffs for debugging.

When an endpoint rejects a request, the failure is often a request-shape problem, not a model issue. Inspecting the exact payload helps in reporting bugs to agent projects, providers, or proxy maintainers with precise details.
